summary: planDependentSync's default (non-full) branch (internal/cli/sync.go) orders pending candidates oldest-fetched-first (missing records, whose fetchedAt is the Go zero time.Time, sort before any real timestamp and so come first too), instead of leaving them in parentIDs' lexical id-sort order. With plain presence-checking (no --stale-before) every pending id shares the same zero fetchedAt, so this is a no-op ordering-wise and default-mode behavior is unchanged; it only matters once --stale-before (sync-stale-before-backfill.json) makes "pending" a scattered subset of a much larger id space. This ordering is intentionally scoped to the default branch only -- the --full branch (case full && scopeSince == nil) must stay in stable id-sort order, since its resumability depends on a persisted numeric offset into a consistently-ordered list; reordering by fetchedAt there would corrupt that offset's meaning across calls (a processed record's fetchedAt changes to "now" after being refetched, which would shift its sort position in a fetchedAt-ordered list). Any future regen must preserve this asymmetry: default mode sorts oldest-first, --full mode stays id-sorted for offset stability.
reason: NEW ISSUE 6 from a fifth live post-fix verification sweep: --stale-before's staleness *classification* was independently confirmed correct (cross-referencing fetched_at against actual stored sample resolution showed near-perfect precision), but a --max-parents cap over id-sorted candidates was exhausting itself entirely on a cluster of records that happened to sort early AND had been backfilled moments before the chosen cutoff by an unrelated earlier --full test run -- so two capped calls (100 each) processed 200 already-correct-but-technically-just-inside-the-cutoff records while the ~1600-workout genuinely-stale backlog (scattered elsewhere in the effectively-random hex id space, fetched hours earlier) was never reached. The user's own root-cause theory (an RFC3339-vs-Go-default timestamp format mismatch breaking the comparison) was investigated and ruled out empirically -- a debug script round-tripping real fetched_at values through the driver into time.Time and comparing via .Before() showed correct classification (1647 stale-and-coarse, 1821 fresh-and-full-res, with only ~98 genuine boundary-case records within seconds of the cutoff) -- but that investigation surfaced the real mechanism: candidate *ordering*, not classification.
validated_outcome: go build/vet/test/govulncheck and verify_skill.py all green. New test TestPlanDependentSync_StaleBeforePrioritizesOldestFirstUnderCap uses a fixture where the oldest stale record deliberately has the lexically-last id (opposite of id-sort order), so an id-ordered bug and the correct oldest-first result produce visibly different outcomes. Live-verified against the user's real account end-to-end through the full sync command (not just the planning function): a scoped run of `sync --resources performance --stale-before 2026-08-14T14:07:43Z --max-parents 5` correctly selected 5 of the genuinely-oldest stale records (fetched 2026-08-13, previously 7-55 samples on 300-2700s workouts, ~1/45-50 downsampling ratio matching BLOCKING #1's original bug) and repaired all 5 to full resolution (samples now within 1-5 of duration) -- the exact ids previously misidentified as unreachable by the pre-fix ordering.
